analysis.one_liner: Requires the largest social media and messaging platforms to let users move data and communicate across competing apps.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, introduced in July 2023 with two Democrats and two Republicans behind it, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Commerce Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The ACCESS Act would require the very largest online platforms—those with more than 100 million U.S. users that make money from user data—to build open doors for their customers. Users could take their data with them when they leave, message people on rival apps without switching, and hire an authorized agent to manage their account. The Federal Trade Commission would write the rules and enforce them, and violators would face penalties counted per affected user.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary users of the biggest social networks, messaging apps, and similar services. Today, leaving a dominant platform means leaving your photos, contacts, and history behind, and there is no way to message a friend on one app from another. The bill would force the giants to let users port their data to competitors and connect across services, making it far easier to switch to a rival if the incumbent raises prices, degrades quality, or mishandles privacy [S2]. Smaller and would-be competitors would gain a foothold because they could interoperate with the giants instead of having to build everything from scratch [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of dominant social and messaging platforms

how_it_helps.text: Large platforms (over 100 million U.S. monthly users earning income from user data) must maintain interfaces that let users securely transfer their data to themselves or to a competing provider in a machine-readable format [S2].

Large platforms must maintain interfaces allowing interoperable communications with users of competing services on fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory terms, and cannot change interfaces with the purpose or effect of blocking those rivals [S2].

Users may designate a registered custodial third-party agent to manage their account, content, and settings on their behalf, and the FTC must set verification rules and can deregister agents that misuse access [S2].

The FTC enforces violations as unfair or deceptive practices, must regularly assess compliance, must consider each affected user an individual violation when fining, and has authority over common carriers for this purpose [S2].
The National Institute of Standards and Technology must publish model technical standards for interoperable messaging, multimedia sharing, and social networking within 180 days of enactment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The handful of giant platform companies—social networks, messaging services, and similar consumer-facing platforms above the 100-million-user threshold—bear the cost of building and maintaining open interfaces, exposing their systems to outside access, and complying with FTC oversight. Their current advantage of holding users' networks and data would shrink [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Big social media and messaging platforms

drawbacks.text: Opening platform interfaces to competitors and third-party agents creates privacy and security risk: more access points for user data means more chances for leaks or abuse, which the bill tries to manage with security standards, FTC registration of agents, and revocation of access for bad actors [S2].
The bill lets custodial third-party agents charge users fees for managing accounts, so consumers who use delegated management could face new charges [S2].

The bill allows platform providers to assess reasonable fees on competitors that exceed usage thresholds, which could raise costs for smaller entrants, though fees must be proportional to the platform's cost of providing access [S2].

Compliance could be expensive for the covered platforms, and the FTC must issue implementing regulations within a year; the act takes effect only once those regulations are issued, which could delay any benefits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: the biggest platforms' dominance rests partly on lock-in—your friends and your data are already there—and the bill attacks that directly by mandating portability and cross-app messaging. The main risks are security and privacy exposure from more third-party access, and the possibility that implementation rules get slow or watered down. The bill includes guardrails (FTC registration, security standards, fee proportionality) but its success would depend heavily on how the FTC writes the rules.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced it and sent it to the Commerce Committee in July 2023, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA) introduced the ACCESS Act on July 26, 2023, joined by Sens. Blumenthal (D-CT), Klobuchar (D-MN), Graham (R-SC), and Hawley (R-MO) [S2].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction [S4].
No further action was ever recorded: the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The giant platform companies, which never had to open their networks to competitors or give up control of user data, and whose lock-in advantage over users remains intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The largest social media and messaging platforms

sides.party_line_note: The bill was notably bipartisan at introduction—two Democrats and two Republicans signed on as original cosponsors—so its death in committee was not a straightforward party-line refusal.

industries.industry: Large social media, messaging, and online platform companies (over 100 million U.S. users monetizing user data)
industries.note: The bill would force these firms to build open interfaces for data portability, cross-service interoperability, and delegated account management, directly eroding the network lock-in that keeps their users from leaving. Because their dominant position lets them charge advertisers more and face less competitive pressure, their interest runs against consumers who want easier switching [S2].

Competing providers would get access to interoperability interfaces and ported user data, letting them offer compatible services without rebuilding networks from scratch. Their gain comes from the same easier switching that benefits users [S2].

The bill would create a new class of FTC-registered agents authorized to manage users' accounts, which could charge users fees. A new service market opens, but consumers using it would pay for it [S2].

industries.industry: Digital advertising and data brokerage ecosystem
industries.note: Platforms that monetize user data are the bill's target, and easier switching plus non-commercialization rules on data obtained through interfaces would constrain how tightly user data can be locked into ad ecosystems. The effect on the broader data economy is indirect and uncertain [S2].
